title: Chapter 12.  Insurgency, Militancy & the Security Situation — Historical Overview

blocks.content: This chapter provides essential factual background on the armed insurgency that began in J&K in the late 1980s, its causes and evolution, and the special security-legal framework introduced in response — presented as a factual historical/administrative overview rather than a political argument, given the topic's continuing sensitivity.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The insurgency has historical roots originating in the late 1980s.
A specialized legal and security framework operates to manage militancy and public order.
Understanding long-term trends is essential for analyzing shifts in the security situation.
Quick revision of key historical milestones provides an accurate security assessment.

blocks.content: An organised, armed insurgency in the Kashmir Valley began in the late 1980s, following a period of political discontent that included allegations of large-scale rigging in the 1987 J&K state assembly elections — an event widely cited by analysts across the political spectrum as a significant catalyst that pushed some disaffected youth (including future militant leaders) toward armed struggle rather than electoral politics.

Militant groups that emerged in this period included the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF), initially advocating for an independent Kashmir, and subsequently a range of Pakistan-based and Pakistan-supported groups (including Hizbul Mujahideen, Lashkar-e-Taiba, and Jaish-e-Mohammed) that generally advocated for Kashmir's accession to Pakistan or, in some cases, a broader pan-Islamist agenda; India has consistently maintained that these groups received substantial training, arming, and logistical support from Pakistan, a charge Pakistan has denied while describing its role as limited to political/diplomatic and moral support for what it terms indigenous self-determination.
Insurgency, Militancy & the Security Situation — Historical Overview

The 1990s saw a sharp escalation in violence, including a mass exodus of the Kashmiri Pandit community (the Valley's Hindu minority) from the Kashmir Valley beginning in early 1990, amid targeted killings and threats — an event of major social and demographic consequence that remains a significant and sensitive subject in Kashmir's contemporary social history, discussed further in Chapter 19 (Demography & Society).

★ EXAM POINT: The alleged rigging of the 1987 J&K Assembly election is widely cited across mainstream historical and political-science accounts (not a fringe claim) as a key catalyst for insurgency, though the insurgency's causes are multi-causal — including broader political alienation, external support, and regional geopolitics — and candidates should present this as one significant contributing factor rather than a single, sole cause.

cells: Armed Forces (Jammu and Kashmir) Special Powers Act, 1990 (AFSPA)

Grants the armed forces special powers (including powers of arrest, search, and use of force in specified circumstances) in areas declared 'disturbed areas' by the Governor/Central Government; has been a subject of sustained human-rights advocacy and political debate over its scope and safeguards
A preventive-detention law allowing detention without trial for specified periods, used in the security context and separately criticised by human-rights organisations for its scope
A central anti-terrorism law applicable across India, frequently invoked in J&K-related prosecutions

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: AFSPA in J&K is a UT/state-specific enactment (the 'Armed Forces (Jammu and Kashmir) Special Powers Act, 1990'), legally distinct from — though similar in structure and purpose to — the separate Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958, which applies in parts of India's North-East. Candidates should not conflate the two as the same statute, even though they share a name and function.

Levels of militancy-related violence in J&K have fluctuated significantly over the past three-plus decades, with periods of relatively higher intensity (notably the 1990s and early 2000s) followed by phases of relative decline, influenced by security operations, political developments (including periodic ceasefires and peace initiatives), and changes in cross-border infiltration patterns.

Various rounds of formal and informal dialogue — between India and Pakistan, and separately between the Government of India and various strands of Kashmiri political opinion (including, at different points, talks with separatist groupings under the banner of the All Parties Hurriyat Conference, formed in 1993) — have been attempted at different points, with varying and generally limited durable outcomes.

The security and political situation following the August 2019 abrogation of Article 370 (Chapter 13) and the subsequent years is addressed specifically and separately in Chapter 29 (Current Developments), since this represents a distinct and more recent phase requiring its own dedicated, up-to-date treatment.
Organised insurgency began in the Kashmir Valley in the late 1980s; the 1987 J&K Assembly election (alleged rigging) is widely cited as a key catalyst.
Major militant groups: JKLF (initially pro-independence), Hizbul Mujahideen, Lashkar-e-Taiba, Jaish-e-Mohammed (broadly pro-Pakistan-accession/pan-Islamist).
Kashmiri Pandit exodus from the Valley began in early 1990 — a major, sensitive demographic event (see Chapter 19).
AFSPA (J&K), 1990 is a distinct enactment from the separate AFSPA, 1958 applicable in North-East India.
All Parties Hurriyat Conference formed in 1993, an umbrella grouping of separatist political opinion, party to various rounds of dialogue over the years.
